alternatives.why_less_likely: Although pool_exhausted errors appear in inventory, they start after the initial capacity saturation and are a consequence of workers being pinned; the root trigger is the capacity saturation itself.

causal_chain.claim: Inventory reached capacity saturation with all workers busy and requests queuing.
Due to inventory saturation, orders' calls to inventory began timing out or receiving pool_exhausted errors.
Orders started returning 503 errors to the gateway when inventory calls failed.
Gateway converted upstream 503 errors into internal_error responses to clients, producing the sustained burst of failures.

root_cause.summary: Inventory exhausted its worker pool, causing requests to queue and eventually fail, which propagated upstream to produce gateway errors.

verification.reason: no replayable condition matches this hypothesis

alternatives.why_less_likely: Although inventory showed increased latency, the root cause was pool exhaustion rather than intrinsic slowness, as shown by explicit pool_exhausted errors.
Orders did retry, but the retries were a consequence of inventory failures; the primary driver was inventory pool exhaustion.

causal_chain.claim: Inventory service exhausted its DB connection pool, causing pool_exhausted errors.
Inventory latency increased, evidenced by slow request warnings with rising duration.
Orders service received 503 errors from inventory due to inventory failures.
Gateway service received 503 errors from orders due to order failures.
User-visible symptom: gateway began returning 5xx errors, as shown in metrics.

root_cause.summary: Inventory service exhausted its DB connection pool, causing pool_exhausted errors and increased latency.
